title: Version Control with Git: Tracking Every Change

questions.question: What exactly is a Git commit?
options: A zipped backup of the whole folder
An immutable snapshot of the staged files plus author, message, and a pointer to the previous commit
A branch that cannot be deleted
An automatic upload to the remote server
questions.rationale: A commit records the state of the staged files together with author, timestamp, message, and parent pointer, identified forever by its hash.

questions.question: git add moves changes from:
options: The staging area to history
The remote to your local repository
The working directory to the staging area
The local repository to the remote
questions.rationale: git add stages edits from the working directory; the later git commit takes the snapshot from staging into history.

questions.question: Why does Git have a staging area at all?
options: It lets you commit selected changes, keeping one logical change per commit
It speeds up the network connection
It stores deleted files forever
It is required before any git log can run
questions.rationale: The index lets you hand-pick which edits form the next commit, even when the working directory mixes several unrelated changes.

questions.question: Why is git revert preferred over git reset --hard for commits others already have?
options: revert deletes all later commits, which is tidier
revert creates a new commit that undoes an old one, so shared histories stay consistent
They are identical commands with different flags
reset --hard fails on private branches only
questions.rationale: revert rewrites nothing: it adds a compensating commit, while reset --hard erases history that teammates may already depend on.

questions.question: A Git branch is best described as:
options: A full copy of every file in the project
A network request to the server
A movable label pointing at a commit
A compressed archive in .git/objects
questions.rationale: A branch is just a 41-byte pointer file that moves as you commit — which is why creating one is effectively free.

questions.question: A merge conflict happens when:
options: Two branches exist at the same time
Both branches changed the same lines of a file differently
A commit has no message
The remote server is unreachable
questions.rationale: Git merges different-line changes automatically; only competing edits to the same lines require a human to resolve.

questions.question: The correct way to finish resolving a merge conflict is:
options: Delete the repository and clone again
Run git push immediately
Edit the file to the text you want, remove the conflict markers, git add it, then commit
Run git merge again on the same branch
questions.rationale: Resolution means producing the final text without <<<<<<< markers, staging it with git add, and committing to complete the merge.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Git and GitHub?
options: GitHub is the offline version of Git
Git is a website; GitHub is a program
They are the same product from different vendors
Git is the open-source version control tool; GitHub is a hosting platform built on it
questions.rationale: Git runs on your machine and works with any server; GitHub adds hosting plus issues, pull requests, and review on top.

questions.question: git fetch differs from git pull because fetch:
options: Also merges remote changes into your branch
Downloads remote commits without merging, letting you inspect them first
Pushes local commits to the remote
Deletes commits the remote no longer has
questions.rationale: pull is fetch plus merge in one step; fetch alone downloads new commits so you can review before integrating.

questions.question: What does a .gitignore file do?
options: Tells Git which untracked files or patterns to never track, such as build output and .env
Hides files from your text editor
Encrypts the listed files
Compresses the repository database
questions.rationale: Patterns in .gitignore keep machine-generated and secret files out of version control; tracked files must be untracked before the rule applies.
